note: "as they would that of few others" was strengthened to "above almost any other".
replacement: “I affirm, then, that in going there you leave many enemies behind you here, and bring more back with you. Perhaps you imagine that the treaty you have made can be trusted. So long as you keep quiet it will go on existing in name (for in name only it has become, through the practices of certain men here and at Sparta). But if you suffered a serious reverse anywhere, our enemies would not hesitate a moment to attack us. The reason is, first, that disaster forced the convention on them and it brought them less honor than it brought us; and second, that the convention itself contains many points still in dispute. Again, some of the most powerful states have never accepted the arrangement at all. Some of them are at open war with us. Others are held back only by truces renewed every ten days, since the Lacedaemonians have not yet moved. And it is only too probable that if they saw our power divided, as we are hurrying to divide it, they would attack us with vigor, together with the Siceliots, whose alliance they would once have valued as they would that of few others. A man ought therefore to weigh these points. He ought not to think of gambling with a country in so critical a position, or of reaching for another empire before we have made the one we hold secure. The Thracian Chalcidians, after all, have been in revolt from us all these years and are still not subdued, and others on the continents obey us only doubtfully. Meanwhile our allies the Egestaeans have been wronged, and we hurry to their help, while the rebels who have wronged us for so long are still waiting for their punishment.
